# The scripts

[Walkthrough index](../README.md) · [The operating skills](operating-skills.md) · [Take it to production](take-it-to-production.md)

Every script stage 00 seeds into your config repo, with what it does, how it is called and an example: the page form of `./scripts/help`, read off the same headers that `<name> --help` prints. Run any of them from the repo root as `./scripts/<name>`. The families are the name prefixes; the [scripts README](../seed/scripts/README.md) has the long-form table and the header layout a new script follows.

## The fleet's lifecycle

Create, point and delete the kind clusters; every rebuild drill is these three in order.

### `cluster-down`

Delete a local kind cluster. Everything comes back from git; that is the point.

```text
Delete the local kind cluster. Everything comes back from git - that's the point.

Usage:
  CLUSTER_NAME=<name> cluster-down

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Environment:
  CLUSTER_NAME  the cluster to delete (default ggp-local-01)

Examples:
  # the platform cluster
  ./scripts/cluster-down
  # a spoke
  CLUSTER_NAME=ggp-prod-01 ./scripts/cluster-down

See also: cluster-up; cluster-sync; every act checkpoint's drill 1
```

### `cluster-sync`

Point a cluster at its folder: install the pinned Flux, mint its deploy key, apply the sync.

```text
What `flux bootstrap` does, minus the part where it pushes to main - nothing does (rule
1.3).

<cluster-path> is the folder under clusters/ whose flux-system/ was landed by PR at stage 03
(e.g. clusters/platform/local-01). --write mints a read-write deploy key (stage 14's robot).
The old key of the same title is always replaced; the manifests in git - extra components
included - take over at the first sync, so there are no bootstrap flags to remember across
rebuilds. On a cluster already syncing itself the install is skipped (git's components file
is the authority and the CLI refuses to install over a self-managed Flux) and the run is a
key rotation.

Usage:
  cluster-sync <cluster-path> [--context <ctx>] [--write]

Arguments:
  cluster-path  the folder under clusters/ whose flux-system/ was landed by PR (e.g.
                clusters/platform/local-01)

Options:
  --context <ctx>  the kube context to sync (default: the current one)
  --write          mint a read-write deploy key: the robot's privilege (stage 14), platform
                   cluster only
  -h, --help       this text

Examples:
  # a spoke, read-only key
  ./scripts/cluster-sync clusters/dev/dev-01 --context kind-ggp-dev-01
  # the platform cluster, the robot's key
  ./scripts/cluster-sync clusters/platform/local-01 --context kind-ggp-local-01 --write

See also: rule 1.3; stages 03 and 14; the deploy keys as the forge's witness (Act II checkpoint)
```

### `cluster-up`

Create a local kind cluster for a class, on the node image its class pins.

```text
Create the local kind cluster for gitops-golden-path. Detects docker or podman; fails early
with a named missing tool.

Usage:
  CLASS=<platform|dev|prod> CLUSTER_NAME=<name> HTTP_PORT=<n> HTTPS_PORT=<n> cluster-up

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Environment:
  CLASS                  the class whose pin in clusters/versions.yaml picks the node image
                         (default platform)
  CLUSTER_NAME           the kind cluster name (default ggp-local-01)
  HTTP_PORT, HTTPS_PORT  host ports for the ingress (default 8080, 8443)
  KIND_NODE_IMAGE        override the image; unset means the class pin

Examples:
  # the platform cluster
  ./scripts/cluster-up
  # the prod spoke
  CLASS=prod CLUSTER_NAME=ggp-prod-01 HTTP_PORT=8082 HTTPS_PORT=8445 ./scripts/cluster-up

See also: clusters/versions.yaml; stage 07; cluster-down; cluster-sync
```

## Stage checkpoints

Is my fleet green: one script per stage, PASS/FAIL per claim, the same file CI runs.

### `checkpoint-02`

Stage 02 checkpoint: labeled, self-judging checks over the rendered output.

```text
Every line is PASS/FAIL + what it means; exits non-zero if anything failed. CI runs this
exact script - the checkpoint and the pipeline can never disagree.

Usage:
  checkpoint-02

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # PASS/FAIL per claim, exit 1 on any FAIL
  ./scripts/checkpoint-02

See also: stage 02; layout-gate
```

## Toolchain and ladder checks

Are my tools and pins right: every check-* script, and check runs them all.

### `check`

The umbrella toolchain gate: are my tools the pinned ones, in one command.

```text
Pure composition - runs every check-* script in this folder and aggregates. Individual
scripts remain first-class for event-driven use (flux bump -> check-kustomize-flux-parity +
check-helm-flux-parity; dev-rung upgrade -> check-version-ladder). Cluster-state gates
(checkpoint-NN) are deliberately NOT included: "is my toolchain right" and "is my fleet
green" are different questions and deserve different exit codes.

Usage:
  check

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # every check-* script here, aggregated; exit 1 if any failed
  ./scripts/check

See also: every check-* script; checkpoint-NN for cluster state, which this deliberately excludes
```

### `check-flux-aks-parity`

Does the local Flux CLI match the Flux release bundled in AKS's microsoft.flux extension?

```text
The Act VIII claim - "AKS absorbs what you built by hand" - is only honest if the local and
managed Flux versions agree. Scrapes Microsoft's release notes (newest entry first); a
scrape is fragile by nature, so failures WARN rather than block, and the page is the
fallback: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-arc/kubernetes/flux-gitops-release-notes

Usage:
  check-flux-aks-parity

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # PASS on the same minor line; WARN if the scrape breaks
  ./scripts/check-flux-aks-parity

See also: rule 4.3; stage 00; Act VIII
```

### `check-helm-flux-parity`

Does the helm CLI match the helm library helm-controller embeds?

```text
The helm<->flux parity gate: the helm CLI is a render tool (chart authoring, `helm
template`/`lint`, values verification), so local renders must match what helm-controller
does in-cluster. Same chain as kustomize, with a free mapping: No skew ladder needed: helm's
k8s window (n..n-3) covers the three-rung fleet.

Usage:
  check-helm-flux-parity

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # PASS/FAIL with the pinned install on FAIL
  ./scripts/check-helm-flux-parity

See also: rule 4.1; clusters/versions.yaml; check-kustomize-flux-parity
```

### `check-k8s-aks-parity`

Has AKS's support window moved on without the fleet's version ladder?

```text
The ladder's claim - next/current/stable is exactly what a managed cluster may run (stage
07, rule 4.3) - decays silently: kind runs any minor forever, AKS does not, and nothing else
fails until Act VIII refuses the version. This gate re-derives the window
(scripts/derive-ladder --window) and compares it to the declared ladder. The scrape behind
it is fragile by nature, so scrape failures WARN rather than block, same as
check-flux-aks-parity.

Usage:
  check-k8s-aks-parity

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # PASS per class inside the window; FAIL names the rung
  ./scripts/check-k8s-aks-parity

See also: rule 4.3; derive-ladder; stage 16
```

### `check-kustofmt-kustomize-parity`

Does the installed kustofmt link the kyaml the pinned kustomize ships?

```text
The kustofmt<->kustomize parity gate: the house style is "what kustomize emits", and that is
only true while kustofmt links the kyaml the pinned kustomize ships. kustofmt is released
one build per kyaml (its compatibility.yaml maps every kustomize release to the kustofmt
built from the same library), so the pin is a lookup, not a guess. kustofmt installs
natively (a writer under -w and a hook on every commit: the operator side of rule 4.2 wins),
so this gate also hands out the install, as the other check-* gates do. Two readings that
must agree: The binary is asked rather than the table because a packaging-only release adds
no row; the table is asked for kustomize because nothing installed can say it.

Usage:
  check-kustofmt-kustomize-parity

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # PASS/FAIL with the pinned install on FAIL
  ./scripts/check-kustofmt-kustomize-parity

See also: rule 3.4; style-gate; clusters/versions.yaml
```

### `check-kustomize-flux-parity`

Does the local kustomize render like kustomize-controller's effective library?

```text
The kustomize<->flux parity gate: local `kustomize build` must render like the cluster does.
The cluster renders with kustomize-controller's EFFECTIVE kustomize library - the go.mod
replace directive wins over the require line - so version strings are not the truth; the
dependency graph is. This script walks it: and compares the installed kustomize, handing out
the pinned install if wrong.

Usage:
  check-kustomize-flux-parity

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # PASS/FAIL with the pinned install on FAIL
  ./scripts/check-kustomize-flux-parity

See also: rule 4.1; clusters/versions.yaml
```

### `check-ladder-due`

What the ladder owes: every ascent in progress, judged against soak.yaml's min and max.

```text
Below min the line reads SOAKING, between the two DUE, past max FAIL, and FROZEN when the
freeze calendar covers the rung's paths today. The prefix puts it in ./scripts/check, so
every stage start and every checkpoint prints it; a fleet runs it on a schedule (stage 27).
The logic lives in soak-gate, which judges min at the PR; this is its --due mode.

Usage:
  check-ladder-due

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # SOAKING, DUE, FAIL past max, FROZEN by the calendar, HELD by a closed item
  ./scripts/check-ladder-due
  # the same, and a work item per due ascent that has none
  ./scripts/soak-gate --due --items

See also: soak-gate (the logic); soak.yaml; freezes.yaml; rule 5.7; stage 16
```

### `check-repo`

Is this repository still configured the way day zero said?

```text
PASS/FAIL per setting, exit 1 on any FAIL. Reads back the merge policy (rule 1.2), the main
ruleset (1.3), the seeded files (1.4, 2.2), this clone's local settings, and the backlog
(2.5). Run it at stage 00 after seeding, and whenever you doubt the repo - a real platform
repo keeps it.

Usage:
  check-repo

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # PASS/FAIL per setting; run it after seeding and whenever you doubt the repo
  ./scripts/check-repo

See also: rules 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 2.2, 2.5; ruleset; stage 00
```

### `check-sops-flux-parity`

Do the sops and age CLIs match the libraries kustomize-controller decrypts with?

```text
The sops<->flux parity gate: what the sops CLI encrypts, kustomize-controller must decrypt -
and the controller decrypts with the sops library EMBEDDED in its go.mod (age likewise, via
filippo.io/age). Cross-version sops history is real (the 3.8 MAC-computation change broke
older decryptors), so a workstation running "latest" writes ciphertext ahead of the fleet's
decryptor. This script walks the graph: and compares the pins in clusters/versions.yaml and
the installed CLIs, handing out the pinned install if wrong.

Usage:
  check-sops-flux-parity

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # PASS/FAIL with the pinned install on FAIL
  ./scripts/check-sops-flux-parity

See also: rule 4.1; clusters/versions.yaml; stage 06
```

### `check-version-ladder`

Does kubectl track the dev class, and is every rung within one minor of it?

```text
The version-ladder gate: the fleet spans three Kubernetes minors by design (platform=next,
dev=current, prod=stable), and kubectl's +/-1 skew means only the MIDDLE rung reaches all
three - so kubectl must track the dev class. Pins live in clusters/versions.yaml; a dev
upgrade PR bumps kubectl there too.

Usage:
  check-version-ladder

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # PASS per rung and per live cluster; FAIL hands out the kubectl install
  ./scripts/check-version-ladder

See also: rule 4.3; clusters/versions.yaml; stages 07 and 16
```

## Act drills

The fleet from nothing, unattended, with the number from artifacts; run-drill runs them and writes the pack.

### `act-1-drill`

Act I drill runner: re-earns the act checkpoint's four numbers, unattended.

```text
DESTRUCTIVE - it deletes and rebuilds the kind cluster, pushes a dated pre-release tag to
the app repo (triggering a GHCR publish), and pushes three real PRs here (pin bump,
deliberate break, revert) and merges them. Guarded by --yes. Timings are extracted from
artifacts (commit stamps, status created_at, condition transitions) - no stopwatch, same
rule as act-checkpoint.md.

Usage:
  act-1-drill
  act-1-drill --yes

Options:
  --yes       run it; bare, the script prints what it would destroy and exits 1
  -h, --help  this text

Environment:
  APP_DIR  the app repo's checkout (default ../gitops-golden-path-app)

Examples:
  # read the blast radius, nothing is touched
  ./scripts/act-1-drill
  # the run; the log is /tmp/act-1-drill.log
  ./scripts/act-1-drill --yes

See also: the Act I checkpoint page; run-drill (the skill that runs this and writes the pack)
```

```text
Usage:

Examples:

  # the run; the log is /tmp/act-2-drill.log

See also: the Act II checkpoint page; run-drill (the skill that runs this and writes the pack); checkpoint-07
```

Act IV drill runner: the fleet from nothing, unattended, with the number from artifacts.

```text
DESTRUCTIVE - it deletes and rebuilds all three kind clusters. Guarded by --yes. "Nothing"

waited Ready, and the key asserted read-write. Timings are extracted from artifacts
(namespace creation stamps, the stamps' own reconcile history) - no stopwatch, same rule as
act-checkpoint.md.

Usage:
  act-4-drill
  act-4-drill --yes

Options:
```

## Gates

One class of evidence, one verdict: the same file as a paste block, in CI and from a hook.

### `base-gate`

Base gate: a change under a base tree may not change what any cluster receives.

```text
Base gate: base is sacred, as a verdict. A change under a base tree (apps/base/,
infrastructure/base/) has no rung to gate it on, so it is allowed only when nothing any
cluster receives changes (rule 5.4, third corollary; the patterns page, "Base is sacred").
Two layers, because the two failure modes have different evidence: A change that touches no
base tree is not this gate's business: OK, exit 0.

Usage:
  base-gate [--subject "<pr title>"] [base-ref] [head-ref]

Arguments:
  base-ref, head-ref  the change to judge (default origin/main HEAD)

Options:
  --subject "<pr title>"  also judge the claim: the title's type must say what the render
                          says
  -h, --help              this text

Examples:
  # the fact alone: every consumed root renders byte-identical on both sides
  ./scripts/base-gate origin/main HEAD
  # fact and claim, as CI's pr-record runs it
  ./scripts/base-gate --subject "refactor(base): absorb the dev patch" origin/main HEAD

See also: rule 5.4; the patterns page (base is sacred); stage 21
```

### `commit-gate`

The commit convention as a verdict: one grammar, four ways in.

```text
The point of --docs is that the course cannot teach a convention it does not follow. Every
`git commit -m`, `gh pr create --title`, `pr-open <branch> "<subject>"` and
`--commit-template` string in the walkthrough is extracted and judged by the SAME grammar
that judges real commits, so "the docs drifted" is a failing check rather than a thing
someone notices in year two.

Grammar and rules: appendices/commit-convention.md in the course repo

Usage:
  commit-gate --docs [files...]
  commit-gate --range <rev-range>
  commit-gate --file <path>
  commit-gate --subject "<subject>" ["<body>"]

Options:
  --docs [files...]        every commit message the walkthrough tells a reader to type
                           (default: the whole course)
  --range <rev-range>      real commits, e.g. origin/main..HEAD
  --file <path>            one message file: the commit-msg hook's argument
  --subject "<t>" ["<b>"]  one subject and optional body: the PR-title check
  -h, --help               this text

Examples:
  # a PR title before pr-open sees it
  ./scripts/commit-gate --subject "promote(app-prod): app 0.1.2" "Refs: #9"
  # the branch
  ./scripts/commit-gate --range origin/main..HEAD

See also: appendices/commit-convention.md; rule 2.1; the commit-msg hook (stage 11)
```

### `freeze-gate`

Is this change trying to land inside a customer's change freeze?

```text
A freeze is a MERGE-TIME control, not a runtime one. The naive implementation - `flux
suspend kustomization` - stops the reconciler, and the CR's own API doc says what that
means: "suspend subsequent kustomize executions". ALL of them, including drift correction.
So a suspended stamp no longer repairs a hand-edited Deployment, which makes the freeze
window the least safe window of the year. It also never expires, blocks the emergency fix
you actually need, and leaves no record of who froze what or why.

What a customer freeze actually wants is narrower: do not put NEW VERSIONS into my
production between these dates. That is a question about which commits may merge, so it is
answered where merges are decided - in a required check, against a calendar in git. Expiry
is then structural rather than remembered: the window has an end date.

Override: a `Freeze-override: <reason>` trailer on any commit in the range. Deliberately
possible and deliberately loud - a freeze nobody can override is one people bypass by
turning the check off, which is worse than an override with a reason attached to it.

Usage:
  freeze-gate [base-ref] [head-ref]
  freeze-gate --calendar
  freeze-gate --at <YYYY-MM-DD> [base-ref] [head-ref]

Arguments:
  base-ref, head-ref  the change to judge (default origin/main HEAD)

Options:
  --calendar   what is frozen now, and what is coming
  --at <date>  evaluate as of a date, for planning and tests
  -h, --help   this text

Environment:
  FREEZE_CALENDAR   the calendar file (default freezes.yaml)
  FREEZE_WARN_DAYS  days ahead a coming freeze is flagged (default 7)

Examples:
  # the calendar
  ./scripts/freeze-gate --calendar
  # a PR against it
  ./scripts/freeze-gate origin/main HEAD

See also: stage 27; declare-freeze (the skill); the Freeze-override: trailer
```

### `issue-gate`

Does this change cite a work item that exists, and is open? PASS/FAIL per issue.

```text
PASS/FAIL per issue, exit 1 on any FAIL.

Reads the Closes:/Refs: trailers (rule 2.5) - one per line, `Refs: #9` or `Refs: #9, #12`.
Every number must be an issue in THIS repo (not a pull request) and, before the merge, open:
a closed work item is finished work, and a change citing it is a change nobody asked for.

Usage:
  issue-gate [--landed] "<body>"
  issue-gate [--landed] --file <path>

Arguments:
  body  a PR body or commit message with its Refs:/Closes: trailers

Options:
  --file <path>  read the body from a file
  --landed       the change has merged: a closed item is fine, the merge may have closed it
  -h, --help     this text

Environment:
  GH_REPO  the repository (default: the one gh sees)

Examples:
  # a body before pr-open
  ./scripts/issue-gate "$(cat body.md)"
  # the merge, as CI's push run judges it
  ./scripts/issue-gate --landed "$(git log -1 --format=%B)"

See also: rule 2.5; pr-open; CI's pr-record job
```

### `layout-gate`

Layout gate: one resource per file, named <name>.<kind>.yaml, in a typed folder.

```text
Layout gate: rules 3.1 and 3.2 as a verdict. One resource per file; the file is
<metadata.name>.<kind>.yaml, lowercase, dots in the name written as dashes (patches
<target>.<kind>.patch.yaml, replacements <target>.<kind>.replacement.yaml); and it sits in a
typed folder: resources/, patches/, replacements/ or secrets/.

Judged over the resource trees only: apps/ infrastructure/ clusters/ policy/ tenants/. Not
judged: kustomization.yaml (tool-mandated), flux-system/ (tool-managed, rewritten on every
re-bootstrap), clusters/versions.yaml (a pin file, not a resource), and anything under
config/, which holds generator inputs beside their kustomization (rule 3.2). A JSON6902
patch is an op list with no kind inside, so for it and for a replacement spec the filename
alone names the target; a strategic-merge patch and every resource must agree with their own
kind and metadata.name.

Needs yq and nothing else, so checkpoint-02 runs it from stage 02; style-gate runs it first
from stage 11, which puts it in the pre-commit hook and CI without another line.

Usage:
  layout-gate [files...]

Arguments:
  files  the files to judge (default: every tracked YAML under the resource trees)

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # the whole tree
  ./scripts/layout-gate
  # one file
  ./scripts/layout-gate apps/base/app/resources/app.deployment.yaml

See also: rules 3.1 and 3.2; style-gate and checkpoint-02, which run it
```

### `path-gate`

Which protected paths does a change touch, and what does that mean for review?

```text
Reports; it does not block - blocking is branch protection's job (stage 21 step 2).

Usage:
  path-gate [base-ref] [head-ref]

Arguments:
  base-ref, head-ref  the change to read (default origin/main HEAD)

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # a branch
  ./scripts/path-gate origin/main HEAD

See also: rule 5.4; CODEOWNERS; stage 21
```

### `policy-gate`

Rendered-standards gate: every overlay rendered and judged against policy/ with conftest.

```text
A pure function over the working tree - no cluster, no credentials - so this SAME file runs
locally as a paste block, in CI, and (stage 11) from a pre-push hook: one verdict, three
venues. PASS/FAIL contract as always.

Usage:
  policy-gate

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # the same verdict as CI and the pre-push hook
  ./scripts/policy-gate

See also: rule 5.6; stage 08; policy/
```

### `revert-gate`

Would this change drag credentials backwards, or undo a commit marked as not revertable?

```text
Two checks, because the two failure modes have different evidence: Check 1 cannot be
forgotten and is the authority. Check 2 is the author's knowledge on top - it catches what a
path scan cannot see, like a cluster that no longer exists.

Usage:
  revert-gate [base-ref] [head-ref]

Arguments:
  base-ref, head-ref  the change to judge (default origin/main HEAD)

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # a revert branch
  ./scripts/revert-gate origin/main HEAD

See also: rule 5.10; commit convention rule 9; stage 20
```

### `slo-gate`

SLO gate: did the rung meet its SLO over the soak window? The promotion ladder's second signature.

```text
SLO gate: the promotion ladder's second signature. Convergence evidence (green status
contexts) says a rung is Ready; this says the rung MET ITS SLO over its soak window. Refuses
the next rung while the error budget is burning - and refuses on NO TRAFFIC too: absence of
evidence is not health. Clusters are the remote-writing spokes (dev-01, prod-01): the hub's
own series carry no cluster label, because externalLabels are applied on egress, not to
local storage.

Usage:
  slo-gate <cluster> [window]

Arguments:
  cluster  a remote-writing spoke: dev-01 or prod-01
  window   the evidence window (default 30m)

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Environment:
  SLO_TARGET     availability target (default: read from the SLO rule in git)
  SLO_P95_MAX    p95 latency ceiling in seconds (default 0.3)
  SLO_MIN_SOAK   residency the candidate must have (default: soak.yaml's min, else 2m)
  SLO_STAMP      the stamp to judge (default app-<env>)
  SLO_GATE_PORT  the local port for the hub port-forward (default 19092)

Examples:
  # before a promotion to prod
  ./scripts/slo-gate dev-01 10m

See also: rule 5.7; stage 09; soak-gate; promote (the skill)
```

### `soak-gate`

Has the artifact this promotion moves served its soak on the rung above? And what does the ladder owe?

```text
A soak is evidence about the artifact, not the copy (pattern 4): the bytes that ran on dev
are the bytes prod receives, so dev's clean window is prod's evidence, and a window has a
length. soak.yaml declares that length per artifact kind and target rung; this gate holds
every ascent to it and reads the time served from git's own dates (rule 5.8): the
first-parent commits that put the candidate on the rung above and kept it there. Nothing
here is a clock somebody started.

Waiver: a `Soak-waived: <reason>` trailer passes a failing verdict, loudly, the way
freeze-gate's override does: a soak nobody can waive is one people bypass by turning the
check off, which is worse than a waiver with a reason in the record.

Two numbers per ascent. min is what the artifact owes before it climbs, judged at the PR.
max is what the rung below owes: how long it may run what the rung above has left behind,
since past that point the rung above tests against a platform the rung below does not run
and its evidence is no longer about it. max is judged by --due, where there is no PR to
refuse: below min a line reads SOAKING, between the two DUE, past max FAIL, and FROZEN when
an active entry in freezes.yaml covers the rung's paths.

Pointers, per kind: the file on a rung, the value, and the rung above. Entry rungs (an image
at dev, a chart or a minor at platform) are pins, not promotions, and owe no soak: that is
where the artifact starts earning one.

Usage:
  soak-gate [--record <file>] [base-ref] [head-ref]
  soak-gate <kind> <rung> [candidate]
  soak-gate --declared
  soak-gate --due [--items]

Arguments:
  base-ref, head-ref  the change to judge: every promotion pointer the diff moves (default
                      origin/main HEAD)
  kind                image | chart | kubernetes
  rung                dev | prod, the rung being promoted to
  candidate           the value being promoted (default: what the rung above serves)

Options:
  --record <file>  a commit message or PR body to read a Soak-waived: trailer from
  --declared       print the declared min and max per ascent
  --due            what the ladder owes: SOAKING, DUE, FAIL past max, FROZEN, HELD (this is
                   check-ladder-due)
  --items          with --due: open a work item per due ascent that has none
  -h, --help       this text

Environment:
  SOAK_FILE  the policy file (default soak.yaml)

Examples:
  # one ascent, before the PR exists
  ./scripts/soak-gate chart dev
  # a branch, as the pre-push hook runs it
  ./scripts/soak-gate origin/main HEAD
  # the report with its work items
  ./scripts/soak-gate --due --items

See also: soak.yaml; check-ladder-due; slo-gate; rule 5.7; stage 16; decision 0040
```

### `style-fix`

Format YAML in place with kustofmt, the format authority behind style-gate.

```text
gofmt's shape: -l lists the files whose bytes differ from the emitted style, -w rewrites
exactly those, so the script can say which files it touched. The binary is the pinned one or
nothing: the pin lives in clusters/versions.yaml and check-kustofmt-kustomize-parity names
the install.

Usage:
  style-fix [files...]

Arguments:
  files  the files to rewrite (default: every tracked YAML outside tool-owned trees)

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # one file after a yq edit
  ./scripts/style-fix .sops.yaml
  # the whole tree
  ./scripts/style-fix

See also: rule 3.4; style-gate; check-kustofmt-kustomize-parity
```

### `style-gate`

Style gate: the YAML convention as a verdict, kustofmt for format and yamllint for the rest.

```text
Both pins are the same in CI, the git hooks (stage 11) and your terminal, so every venue
reaches the identical verdict.

Usage:
  style-gate [files...]

Arguments:
  files  the files to judge (default: every tracked YAML outside tool-owned trees)

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # the whole tree, as CI and the pre-push hook run it
  ./scripts/style-gate
  # the staged files, as the pre-commit hook runs it
  ./scripts/style-gate apps/overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml

See also: rule 3.4; .yamllint.yaml; style-fix; layout-gate
```

## The forge

PRs, reverts, rulesets and the commit a subject names.

### `commit-by-subject`

The sha of the commit whose subject is exactly the one given, on the first-parent line.

```text
Exact, not a substring. `git revert` quotes the subject it undoes, so a substring search
finds the revert (newer, and the opposite event) instead of the break, and an unanchored
version match finds 0.1.10 when you asked for 0.1.1. awk, not grep, so no grep.patternType
setting can reinterpret the parentheses the commit grammar is full of. First-parent, so the
answer is the merge commit (the one that wears statuses), never the branch commit that
shares its title. GitHub appends " (#N)" to a merge commit's subject even under
merge_commit_title: PR_TITLE: a subject given without that suffix matches with the suffix
ignored; one given with it (a revert quotes it) matches verbatim.

Prints the full sha. Exit 1, with a hint on stderr, when nothing matches.

Usage:
  commit-by-subject <subject>
  commit-by-subject --prefix <subject>

Arguments:
  subject  the exact subject; GitHub's ' (#N)' suffix is ignored when you leave it off

Options:
  --prefix    the newest commit whose subject starts with the text
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # the merge that promoted
  ./scripts/commit-by-subject "promote(app-prod): app 0.1.2"
  # the newest break drill
  ./scripts/commit-by-subject --prefix 'break(app-prod): '

See also: rung-time, evidence, pr-revert (all find their commit this way, never by HEAD)
```

### `pr-open`

Open a PR from the staged changes: branch, commit, push, open, and stop there.

```text
The first four steps of rule 2.4 - branch, commit, push, open - and never the fifth. Merging
is your line, after you have read the diff: The subject and body are linted by commit-gate
before anything is created, because the subject becomes the merge commit on main
(merge_commit_title=PR_TITLE) and the body its record (merge_commit_message=PR_BODY). An
empty body is refused: a PR that says nothing is not a deployment record - and a body that
cites no open work item (Refs:/Closes:, rule 2.5) is refused too: a change nobody asked for.
The branch name follows <type>/<issue>/<slug> (rule 2.4), and both segments are checked
against the PR: the type against the subject, the issue against the trailer.

Usage:
  pr-open <branch> "<subject>" [body-file]

Arguments:
  branch     <type>/<issue>/<slug>; the type is checked against the subject, the issue
             against the trailer
  subject    the PR title, which becomes the merge commit's subject
  body-file  the deployment record; stdin when omitted

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # body from a file
  ./scripts/pr-open promote/9/app-prod "promote(app-prod): app 0.1.2" body.md
  # body on stdin
  ./scripts/pr-open fix/12/probe "fix(app-dev): probe path" <<'EOF' ... EOF

See also: rules 2.2 and 2.4; commit-gate; issue-gate; pr-revert
```

### `pr-revert`

Undo a merged PR, by PR: branch, git revert -m 1, push, open, and stop there.

```text
git writes the subject - Revert "<the PR title>" - and it is never rewritten (commit
convention rule 6): that string is the durable link to what it undoes. The body is assembled
from what git already knows plus the one sentence only you know: why now. Merging is your
line, after the diff:

Usage:
  pr-revert [<merge-sha>] "<why now>" ["#<issue>"]

Arguments:
  merge-sha  the merge to undo (default HEAD)
  why now    the one sentence only you know; the rest of the body is assembled from git
  #<issue>   the work item; default: inherited from the reverted merge's trailers

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # the newest merge
  ./scripts/pr-revert "the break drill is over; restore prod"
  # a named merge
  ./scripts/pr-revert 9470bb4 "rolled back after the SLO burned" "#14"

See also: commit convention rule 6; revert-gate; rule 5.10 (secrets roll forward)
```

### `ruleset`

The main ruleset, amended and never replaced; the tags ruleset read back.

```text
Stage 00 created it; later stages add one requirement each, and this is how, so the JSON is
written once and the growth is a log. Stage 00 also created the tags ruleset (immutable once
created); it is never amended.

Checks are not "strict" (the branch need not be up to date with main): a solo repo and the
stage-14 robot would otherwise stall every time main moved under an open PR.

Usage:
  ruleset show
  ruleset require-check <name>...
  ruleset require-owners

Arguments:
  show                     every ruleset: what main requires, that tags are permanent, who
                           may bypass (nobody)
  require-check <name>...  status checks that must pass before a merge (a job's name is its
                           check name)
  require-owners           code-owner review on the paths CODEOWNERS names

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Examples:
  # read it back
  ./scripts/ruleset show
  # a new required check
  ./scripts/ruleset require-check verify

See also: rule 1.3; stages 00, 08, 11, 21; check-repo
```

## Evidence and measures

Numbers from artifacts, never a stopwatch: lead time, detection, DORA, the dossier, what shipped.

### `detect-time`

How long from a break landing in git to the fleet view knowing, from metric samples.

```text
How long from "someone broke prod" to "the fleet view knew" - measured from artifacts.

The answer is a metric sample timestamp: kube-state-metrics reads the stamp's Ready
condition into gotk_resource_info on the hub, so "when did we know" is a query, not a
stopwatch and not a memory. What it prints is the state timeline either side of the break,
which is the same thing your eyes do on the Grafana panel - one line per change.

Deliberately NOT the commit status: a status is a snapshot one reconcile chose to post
(drill 2 met one that was green and said "dependency not ready"). The metric is a continuous
sample of the CR itself. Detection is a metric question; attribution is a status question.
This script answers the first.

The third argument is optional because the commit convention made the DRILL case derivable:
a deliberate break against this stamp has the subject prefix "break(<stamp>): ", so naming
the stamp already selects the commit. A real break is never labelled - it is a feat, a pin,
a promote that happened to hurt - and it is found the other way round: the stamp's
status.history names the revision that failed, and that sha is the anchor. Pass a sha and it
is used as given; pass a subject and it is matched as a prefix.

Usage:
  detect-time <stamp> <kube-context> [break-commit-subject | sha] [window]

Arguments:
  stamp                       the Flux Kustomization, e.g. app-prod
  kube-context                the cluster it runs on, e.g. kind-ggp-prod-01
  break-commit-subject | sha  the break; default: the newest break(<stamp>): commit
  window                      how far back to read (default 1h)

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Environment:
  DETECT_TIME_PORT     the local port for the hub port-forward (default 19097)
  DETECT_TIME_SUSTAIN  seconds a state must hold to count (default 60)

Examples:
  # a drill: the break is labelled
  ./scripts/detect-time app-prod kind-ggp-prod-01

See also: rule 5.8; stage 09; the Act III checkpoint drill 3
```

### `dora`

The four DORA metrics for a GitOps fleet, computed from artifacts, scoped to production.

```text
DORA measures PRODUCTION. All four definitions say so: how often you release to production,
how long a commit takes to reach production, how often a production change fails, how long
production takes to recover. So production is the default scope here and every other rung is
a diagnostic, printed only on request and labelled as not-DORA - because a dev deployment
frequency in the same table is a number someone will quote.

And the UNIT IS THE CHANGE, not the application of the change. One commit reaching fifty
tenants is one deployment, not fifty; a commit that breaks fifty tenants is one failed
change. Counting per-tenant applications makes deployment frequency scale with customer
count - add a customer and look more elite - which is the same class of error as counting
reconciles instead of changes, one level up.

Two signals, because one of them lies. On the hub: A stamp reconciles every commit, so its
revision changes on every push - including pushes that changed nothing it renders. The
workload's generation increments only when the spec actually changed, so that is a
deployment. Both are printed; the gap is the lesson (stage 10).

Production is the LAST RUNG of the ladder, not a cluster name - --production selects it.

Usage:
  dora [--window 30d] [--production <cluster-regex>] [--by tenant|cluster|stamp] [--rungs] [--stages]

Options:
  --window <d>               the period (default 30d)
  --production <regex>       which clusters count as production (default prod)
  --by tenant|cluster|stamp  the breakdown (default tenant)
  --rungs                    add the other rungs as diagnostics, labelled not-DORA
  --stages                   add the lead-time stages per change: soak, review, deploy
  -h, --help                 this text

Environment:
  DORA_PORT     the local port for the hub port-forward (default 19098)
  DORA_STEP     query step in seconds (default 60)
  DORA_SUSTAIN  seconds a state must hold to count (default 90)

Examples:
  # the four numbers over the checkpoint's window
  ./scripts/dora --window 6h
  # with the stages
  ./scripts/dora --window 30d --stages

See also: rule 5.8; stage 10; decision 0022
```

### `evidence`

The auditor's dossier for one commit, from durable artifacts only.

```text
The question this answers, in the checkpoint's words: "between the break and the restore,
what was prod actually running, who fixed it, and how do you know dev was unaffected?"
Memory and scrollback are not evidence. Git, the commit statuses, and the cluster's own
reported revision are - and all three outlive everyone who was on the call.

It derives the blast radius from the commit itself: whichever status context went red names
the stamp and the cluster (kustomization/<stamp>/<cluster>), which is the identifier
alignment rule paying rent - one string, and no lookup table between the alert and the file.

Usage:
  evidence <sha|subject-prefix> [stamp] [kube-context]

Arguments:
  sha|subject-prefix   the commit, or the prefix of its subject
  stamp, kube-context  the blast radius, when the statuses cannot name it

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Environment:
  EVIDENCE_CLUSTER_PREFIX  how kube contexts are named (default kind-ggp-)

Examples:
  # by sha
  ./scripts/evidence 9470bb4
  # the newest break drill
  ./scripts/evidence 'break(app-prod): '

See also: rule 3.6 (identifier alignment); the Act II checkpoint drill 4; audit-evidence (the skill)
```

### `release-notes`

Release notes for one cluster, from what that cluster says it is running.

```text
The premise: a fleet has no single "release". Three clusters share one repo and each is at
its own revision, so "what shipped" is only ever a question about a cluster. Flux already
records the answer - a stamp's .status.lastAppliedRevision is the commit that cluster
actually applied - which makes the range a query rather than a tagging ceremony. No tags, no
release branches, no changelog file to keep honest.

Two views, and the difference is why merge-commit-only matters:

Usage:
  release-notes <stamp> <kube-context> [since] [--first-parent] [--record]

Arguments:
  stamp, kube-context  the stamp and the cluster it runs on
  since                a git revision, or <stamp>@<kube-context> to diff two rungs

Options:
  --first-parent  one line per PR: what shipped, as reviewed
  --record        write the notes as a file under docs/ for a PR
  -h, --help      this text

Environment:
  CLIFF_IMAGE  the pinned git-cliff container (default docker.io/orhunp/git-cliff:2.13.1)

Examples:
  # what prod is running, as reviewed
  ./scripts/release-notes app-prod kind-ggp-prod-01 --first-parent
  # the promotion gap
  ./scripts/release-notes app-prod kind-ggp-prod-01 app-dev@kind-ggp-dev-01 --first-parent

See also: stage 26; promote (the skill reads the gap this way)
```

### `rung-time`

Lead time for one rung: from the commit that asked to the status that says it converged.

```text
The honesty is the point. A commit status has two states and Flux derives them from an
event's severity: an error posts failure, everything else posts success, with the event's
reason as the description. "dependency not ready" is info, so a stamp that reconciles a new
revision before its dependencies have posts a green on that commit seconds after the merge,
before anything is applied. Read that and a promotion looks 4 seconds long when it took 35.
So: wait until the cluster says it applied THIS revision, wait for the rollout, then read
the one status that says "reconciliation succeeded".

Usage:
  rung-time <sha-or-subject> <status-context> <kube-context> <stamp>

Arguments:
  sha-or-subject  the commit, by sha or exact subject
  status-context  the status to read, e.g. kustomization/app-prod/prod-01
  kube-context    the cluster, e.g. kind-ggp-prod-01
  stamp           the Flux Kustomization, e.g. app-prod

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Environment:
  RUNG_BRANCH  the branch the merge landed on (default main)

Examples:
  # the prod rung of a promotion
  ./scripts/rung-time "promote(app-prod): app 0.1.2" kustomization/app-prod/prod-01 kind-ggp-prod-01 app-prod

See also: rule 5.8; every act checkpoint's drill 2; dora
```

### `slo-watch`

Watch a cluster's SLIs move, one line per sample, until Ctrl-C.

```text
The point of the tool is TIME: SLIs are rate() windows, so a break takes ~a minute to show
and a fix takes the window length to clear. Ctrl-C when you have seen what you came for.

Usage:
  slo-watch <cluster> [interval-seconds]

Arguments:
  cluster           a remote-writing spoke: dev-01 or prod-01
  interval-seconds  seconds between samples (default 30)

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Environment:
  SLO_WATCH_PORT  the local port for the hub port-forward (default 19096)

Examples:
  # every 15 seconds
  ./scripts/slo-watch dev-01 15

See also: stage 09; slo-gate
```

## Tools

The rest.

### `derive-ladder`

Derive the Kubernetes version ladder from its authority, AKS's support window.

```text
The authority is AKS's support window (rule 4.3): the three GA minors AKS runs today become
platform=next, dev=current, prod=stable, and the newest kindest/node patch image for each
minor comes from the registry. Scrapes the AKS release calendar; a scrape is fragile by
nature, so a failed parse names the page and stops - nothing falls back to a guess:
https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/supported-kubernetes-versions

Usage:
  derive-ladder
  derive-ladder --window
  derive-ladder --write

Options:
  --window    print just the three minors, newest first
  --write     append the ladder to clusters/versions.yaml; refuses if one exists
  -h, --help  this text

Environment:
  TMPDIR  where the fetched calendar page is kept on a failed parse (default /tmp)

Examples:
  # read before writing
  ./scripts/derive-ladder
  # the window alone, as check-k8s-aks-parity reads it
  ./scripts/derive-ladder --window

See also: rule 4.3; stage 07; check-k8s-aks-parity; stage 16
```

### `refresh-hub-address`

Re-derive the monitoring hub's container IP into every cluster's cluster-facts (fallback path).

```text
FALLBACK PATH: cluster-facts normally name the hub by the platform node's container name
(stage 09 step 2), which survives reboots and rebuilds. Use this only if your environment
does not resolve container names and you pinned the IP instead: a pinned IP is created with
the node container and dies with it, so every reboot or rebuild invalidates the committed
value and the spokes remote-write into nothing. This edits git; you review and commit. (On
AKS this becomes a private endpoint that outlives the cluster - stage 12+.)

Usage:
  refresh-hub-address

Options:
  -h, --help  this text

Environment:
  HUB_NODE  the platform node's container (default ggp-local-01-control-plane)
  HUB_PORT  the hub's NodePort (default 30090)

Examples:
  # only when container names do not resolve in your environment; you review and commit
  ./scripts/refresh-hub-address

See also: stage 09 step 2
```

## The operating skills

Claude Code skills seeded beside the scripts, one runbook each; [the operating skills](operating-skills.md) page says where each fits and where it stops.

| Skill | Arguments | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `/audit-evidence` | `[the question, verbatim] [sha | subject prefix | #PR | <stamp> <cluster> | a date window]` |   Assemble an audit dossier for a change, a PR, a stamp or a time window from durable artifacts only (git, commit statuses, the PR record, the work item, what the cluster applied). Use when someone asks what ran where and when, who approved a change, what evidence gated it, whether a window held any change to production, or for the full evidence trail of one change. Also the closing step of a drill. |
| `/break-glass` | `'[stuck check name | forge down] [incident item #N, created if absent]'` |   Land a production fix when the change machinery itself is the outage (the forge is down, a required check is stuck red), by the narrowest bypass that works, declared on the incident item before acting, with the controls restored and proved afterwards and the change reconciled by PR. Use when asked to bypass a control under incident conditions, or to record a bypass that already happened. |
| `/declare-freeze` | `[<scope> <from>..<to> <reason> <ticket> | lift <id> | nothing, to read the calendar]` |   Declare, shorten or inspect a change freeze as a calendar entry in git (freezes.yaml), checked against the existing calendar and landed by PR. Use when asked to freeze a tenant, a rung or a wave over a window, to lift a freeze early, or to say what is frozen now. Never suspends a reconciler. |
| `/fleet-triage` | `[kustomization/<stamp>/<cluster> | the alert's identifiers | why hasn't my change appeared]` |   Diagnose a red or stuck stamp by the four-layer ladder (fetch, build, apply, health) from the identifier in an alert or status, read what the cluster applied and what the fleet said, and recommend the fix as a PR. Use when a change has not appeared, a stamp is not Ready, a commit wears a red, or a dashboard row is red. Reads only; never applies, edits, scales or suspends. |
| `/onboard-tenant` | `[tenant name or id] [rungs]` |   Onboard a tenant as a replica across the rungs: the tenant leaf per environment, one stamp per (cluster, tenant), the tenant's secret boundary and key, code owners, and the SLO dimension, as one PR with the seven homes of the identifier listed and the isolation proofs. Use when asked to add a tenant, to say what a new tenant needs, or to review a tenant's isolation. |
| `/promote` | `[stamp] [target rung, e.g. app-prod]` |   Open a promotion PR that moves a version up one rung on both signatures (the lower rung's green context and a clean SLO window), with the freeze calendar checked, the blast radius rendered, and a body that is a deployment record. Use when asked to promote, to check whether a rung is ready to promote, or to open the promotion PR. Never merges. |
| `/rotate-secret` | `[<class> key | value <name> | recipient <person> | leak]` |   Rotate a class key, a stored secret value, or a recipient (a person's access) in two phases, overlap then retire, with the revocation step at the provider and the roll-forward trailer, landed as PRs. Use when asked to rotate a key or a value, to remove a person's access, or after a suspected leak. Never commits a new value without a revocation plan. |
| `/run-drill` | `[rebuild <act> | break <stamp> | breach | break-glass | insider | stale | region] [--yes]` |   Run a rebuild drill or a game day (a scripted act drill, a breach rotation, a break-glass, an insider attack on the controls, a stale fleet, a region rebuild) against machinery that already exists, capture the numbers from artifacts, and write the evidence pack on the drill's work item. Use when asked to prove the fleet rebuilds, to run a game day, or to run the quarterly recovery test. |
